proof_nl:
Fix integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n. Then r >= 0 and n-r >= 0, so both quantities [n choose r]_q and [n choose n-r]_q are defined by the given formula

[n choose s]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_s (q;q)_{n-s})

for the relevant values s=r and s=n-r.

Now compute directly from the definition:

[n choose n-r]_q
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_{n-(n-r)})
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r).

Since multiplication is commutative,

(q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r = (q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}.

Therefore

[n choose n-r]_q
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= [n choose r]_q.

So the two defining expressions are identical. Hence the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient is symmetric under replacing r by n-r; in particular, [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q as polynomials in q.
solver_summary: Using only the definition, replace r by n-r and note that n-(n-r)=r. The denominator becomes (q;q)_{n-r}(q;q)_r, which equals (q;q)_r(q;q)_{n-r} by commutativity, so the expressions are identical.
vetter_reason: The proof is a complete direct verification from the stated definition of the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Under 0 <= r <= n, both r and n-r are nonnegative, so both defining expressions are legitimate. Substituting s = n-r into the formula gives [n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r}(q;q)_r), and commutativity of multiplication identifies this denominator with ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), which is exactly the denominator for [n choose r]_q. Hence the two expressions are identical as polynomials in q. There is no reliance on the root theorem or other forbidden dependencies.
